options.B: To accelerate the complete closure of abdominal rectus muscles
options.C: To replace iron lost through physiological lactation diuresis
options.D: To support the metabolic energy required for milk production and tissue repair

explanation: Milk synthesis demands substantial extra calories, proteins, and micronutrients to maintain maternal health and infant growth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h7)

question: Which contraceptive option is safest for a nursing mother who wishes to avoid estrogen-induced drops in milk production?

options.A: Combined oral contraceptive pills
options.B: High-dose estrogen patches
options.C: Estrogen vaginal rings
options.D: Progestin-only contraceptives

explanation: Progestin-only methods do not interfere with breast milk volume or composition, making them ideal during lactation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h8)

question: What criteria must be met for the Lactational Amenorrhea Method to be considered reliable?

options.A: Exclusive breastfeeding, infant under six months, and absence of menses
options.B: Mixed feeding, infant under one year, and irregular menstrual cycles
options.C: Night feeding only, infant under two months, and resumption of periods
options.D: Formula supplementation, infant under three months, and active menses

explanation: LAM relies on frequent suckling to suppress ovulation, which only remains reliable under strict exclusive breastfeeding before six months. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h8)

question: What is a primary function of community health extension workers in post-natal care delivery?

options.A: Performing major emergency surgical interventions
options.B: Prescribing complex psychiatric medications independently
options.C: Managing intensive care blood transfusions in hospitals
options.D: Conducting home visits and identifying postpartum danger signs

explanation: Community workers bridge the gap between facilities and homes by tracking mother-baby pairs and spotting early warning signs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h9)

question: Why is integrating traditional birth attendants into primary health care referral networks beneficial in Nigeria?

options.A: It allows traditional practitioners to perform routine cesarean sections
options.B: It replaces the need for skilled midwives in primary health clinics
options.C: It eliminates the financial costs associated with maternal medications
options.D: It encourages prompt referral of complicated cases to formal health facilities

explanation: Collaboration ensures that women who initially consult traditional attendants are safely directed to hospitals when complications arise. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T52#GNS214_U1_T52_h9)

question: What is the primary purpose of family planning services?

options.A: Mandating a specific family size for community development
options.B: Restricting reproductive choices based on economic status
options.C: Allowing individuals to determine the number and spacing of children
options.D: Eliminating the need for maternal and child healthcare

explanation: Family planning is fundamentally about empowering individuals and couples to freely and responsibly decide the number, spacing, and timing of their children. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h1)

question: How does effective family planning directly impact women's social and economic well-being?

options.A: It guarantees automatic employment in the healthcare sector
options.B: It eliminates the need for financial planning outside of healthcare
options.C: It removes all domestic responsibilities from female heads of households
options.D: It provides opportunities to pursue education and economic activities

explanation: By enabling women to plan their pregnancies, they can better manage their time and health to participate in education, professional development, and economic labor. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h1)

question: What is the minimum recommended birth spacing interval to protect maternal and child health?

options.A: At least twenty-four months apart
options.B: At least five years apart
options.C: No more than twelve months apart
options.D: Exactly six months apart

explanation: Health organizations recommend waiting at least twenty-four months after a live birth before attempting the next pregnancy to reduce maternal and infant risks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h2)

question: A patient asks why her previous closely spaced pregnancy contributed to her current anemia. What physiological mechanism explains this?

options.A: Permanent damage to the bone marrow caused by fetal growth
options.B: Increased iron absorption that paradoxically destroys red blood cells
options.C: Insufficient time for maternal nutritional stores to replenish
options.D: Complete cessation of iron metabolism during the postpartum period

explanation: Pregnancy places a heavy demand on maternal iron and vitamin stores, and a short interval does not allow enough time for these essential reserves to rebuild. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h2)

question: Which contraceptive category relies on a physical block to prevent fertilization?

options.A: Permanent methods
options.B: Behavioral methods
options.C: Barrier methods
options.D: Hormonal methods

explanation: Barrier methods such as condoms, diaphragms, and cervical caps physically stop sperm from meeting the egg. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h3)

question: How do copper intrauterine devices primarily exert their contraceptive effect?

options.A: Creating a local environment toxic to sperm and ova
options.B: Permanently paralyzing the fallopian tube musculature
options.C: Completely shutting down pituitary hormone production
options.D: Accelerating the aging of all circulating oocytes

explanation: The presence of copper induces a sterile inflammatory reaction within the endometrium that impairs sperm motility and viability, preventing fertilization. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h3)

question: What is the primary tool used by healthcare providers to determine the safety of specific contraceptives based on a client's medical history?

options.A: Standardized Obstetric Growth Charts
options.B: Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC)
options.C: National Immunization Schedules
options.D: Primary Health Care Audit Forms

explanation: The WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria provide evidence-based guidance on whether patients with specific medical conditions can safely use various contraceptive methods. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h4)

question: In the GATHER counseling framework, what is the significance of the 'Help' step?

options.A: Helping the provider complete medical paperwork without error
options.B: Providing financial assistance for purchasing the contraceptive
options.C: Physically demonstrating how to administer a surgical procedure
options.D: Assisting the client in making an informed, voluntary decision

explanation: The helping step focuses on guiding the client through their options so they can select the method that best matches their lifestyle, preferences, and health profile. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h4)

question: What action should be avoided immediately after administering a depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection?

options.A: Documenting the procedure in the register
options.B: Applying a clean adhesive bandage
options.C: Instructing the client on return dates
options.D: Massaging the injection site

explanation: Massaging the site after giving DMPA can alter the absorption rate and affect the duration of contraceptive efficacy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h5)

question: A nurse is preparing to insert a copper intrauterine device for a client. What clinical step must always be performed immediately before sounding the uterine cavity?

options.A: Measurement of the client's resting blood pressure
options.B: Administration of a general anesthetic in the clinic
options.C: Immediate removal of all cervical mucous plugs
options.D: Bimanual examination to determine uterine size and position

explanation: A bimanual exam is critical prior to sounding and insertion to evaluate the orientation of the uterus, helping to prevent accidental perforation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h5)

question: What is the most effective initial nursing intervention when a client expresses concern about predictable spotting caused by a newly initiated hormonal contraceptive?

options.A: Scheduling emergency exploratory surgery to find the bleeding source
options.B: Instructing the client to immediately discontinue all medication
options.C: Providing anticipatory guidance and reassurance about normal bleeding changes
options.D: Prescribing high-dose iron supplements without further evaluation

explanation: Explaining expected side effects beforehand helps reduce anxiety and prevents unnecessary discontinuation of effective contraception. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h6)

question: A client using a combined hormonal contraceptive reports sudden, severe unilateral calf pain and swelling. Which complication must the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Iron deficiency anemia
options.B: Pelvic inflammatory disease
options.C: Deep vein thrombosis
options.D: Benign positional vertigo

explanation: Unilateral calf pain and swelling in a client on estrogen-containing contraceptives are classic warning signs of deep vein thrombosis requiring urgent evaluation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h6)

question: Which health workers are often empowered through task-shifting policies to improve contraceptive access in remote Nigerian communities?

options.A: Community Health Extension Workers
options.B: National Health Insurance Auditors
options.C: Hospital Pharmacological Directors
options.D: Consultant Obstetrician Gynecologists

explanation: Task-shifting authorizes Community Health Extension Workers to provide select family planning methods in primary health centers and rural outposts where doctors are scarce. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h7)

question: Why is partnering with traditional rulers and religious leaders vital for successful family planning programs in Nigeria?

options.A: They are legally mandated to purchase all medical contraceptives
options.B: They manage the national drug distribution supply chain
options.C: They hold significant influence over community beliefs and acceptance
options.D: They possess formal clinical training in reproductive medicine

explanation: Involving respected community leaders helps dismantle cultural and religious myths, encouraging broader acceptance and utilization of reproductive health services. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T53#GNS214_U1_T53_h7)

question: What is the primary focus of an Infant Welfare Clinic?

options.A: Inpatient management of chronic adult diseases
options.B: Surgical intervention for congenital defects
options.C: Preventative care and wellness preservation
options.D: Emergency trauma care for pediatric accidents

explanation: Infant Welfare Clinics are specifically designed to keep children healthy through routine monitoring, immunizations, and education rather than treating acute or emergency conditions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h1)

question: Why are Infant Welfare Clinics considered an essential component of primary health care?

options.A: They replace the need for pediatric hospitals in rural and urban settlements.
options.B: They generate significant revenue for local government health departments.
options.C: They provide a direct link between community health needs and formal preventative interventions.
options.D: They serve exclusively as distribution points for prescription medications.

explanation: By operating within communities, these clinics make basic preventative health services easily accessible to families who might otherwise lack healthcare contact. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h1)

question: Which service is a standard component of routine Infant Welfare Clinic visits?

options.A: Growth monitoring and immunizations
options.B: Chemotherapy administration for malignancies
options.C: Inpatient management of severe trauma
options.D: Major pediatric orthopedic surgery

explanation: Tracking physical growth and administering scheduled vaccines are core preventative activities performed during virtually every infant welfare visit. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h2)

question: What is the main rationale for combining multiple preventative services into a single clinic visit?

options.A: It reduces the total number of healthcare personnel required to staff the clinic.
options.B: It eliminates the need for any subsequent follow-up visits during the first year of life.
options.C: It prevents mothers from seeking care at private hospitals or pharmacies.
options.D: It maximizes healthcare contact opportunities for busy caregivers and ensures comprehensive care.

explanation: Bundling services saves time for caregivers and ensures that children receive all necessary preventative interventions simultaneously rather than missing appointments. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h2)

question: What does a flat or downward trajectory on an infant growth chart most commonly indicate?

options.A: Normal genetic acceleration of skeletal length
options.B: Adequate caloric intake and excellent health
options.C: Sub-clinical illness or nutritional deficiency
options.D: A temporary surge in cognitive development

explanation: A stagnant or falling weight curve is frequently the earliest warning sign that a child is experiencing chronic malnutrition or an underlying hidden infection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h3)

question: How do nurses assess developmental milestones during routine clinic visits?

options.A: By performing mandatory computerized neurological scans
options.B: Through direct observation and targeted questioning of the caregiver
options.C: By administering standardized written examinations to toddlers
options.D: Through mandatory blood chemistry and genetic profiling

explanation: Developmental assessment relies on observing how the child interacts and moves during the visit, combined with asking parents about milestones achieved at home. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of maintaining the cold chain in vaccine management?

options.A: To prevent the growth of beneficial bacteria
options.B: To preserve the biological potency of the vaccines
options.C: To accelerate the rate of antibody absorption
options.D: To reduce the financial cost of vaccine transport

explanation: Vaccines are sensitive biological products that lose their effectiveness if exposed to improper temperatures, rendering them useless against infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h4)

question: Why is educating parents about mild post-vaccination side effects an essential nursing responsibility?

options.A: It eliminates the need to record vaccinations on the child health card.
options.B: It cures localized muscle soreness within a few minutes.
options.C: It prevents unnecessary panic and reduces default rates for subsequent doses.
options.D: It guarantees that the child will never contract the target infection.

explanation: When caregivers understand that fever and swelling are normal signs of the immune system responding, they are much more likely to return for booster doses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h4)

question: For how many months is exclusive breastfeeding officially recommended for infants?

options.A: First three months
options.B: First six months
options.C: First twelve months
options.D: First nine months

explanation: Global health guidelines strongly advocate for exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life without any other food or water. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h5)

question: A mother at an infant welfare clinic in a rural Nigerian community asks what foods to introduce when her baby turns six months old. What is the most appropriate nursing guidance?

options.A: Introduce thick, nutrient-dense local complementary foods made from available staples alongside continued breastfeeding.
options.B: Delay all solid food introduction until the child completes their first year of life.
options.C: Feed the child only clear broths and fruit juices until they can chew meat.
options.D: Stop breastfeeding entirely and switch the infant exclusively to diluted cow milk.

explanation: At six months, breast milk is no longer sufficient on its own, so thick, mashed local foods should be introduced while breastfeeding continues. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h5)

question: Which of the following is considered a general danger sign in an infant requiring immediate referral?

options.A: Mild scaling skin on the scalp
options.B: Spitting up small amounts of milk after feeding
options.C: Inability to drink or breastfeed
options.D: Low-grade fever after immunization

explanation: An infant who cannot suck or drink is severely compromised and represents a major danger sign requiring urgent hospital evaluation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of utilizing IMCI guidelines in primary health clinics?

options.A: To systematically identify and manage common childhood illnesses and recognize severe danger signs
options.B: To diagnose complex adult cardiovascular diseases during pediatric visits
options.C: To replace surgical procedures with herbal remedies in rural communities
options.D: To eliminate the need for keeping physical patient health records

explanation: IMCI provides a holistic, standardized framework for primary healthcare workers to assess and treat leading causes of childhood mortality. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h6)

question: Which task is a direct clinical responsibility of the nurse during an infant welfare session?

options.A: Constructing physical buildings for primary health centers
options.B: Manufacturing routine pharmaceutical vaccines in a laboratory
options.C: Procuring international funding for health ministries
options.D: Performing clinical assessments and administering scheduled vaccines

explanation: Nurses directly examine infants, evaluate their development, and give vaccines as part of routine clinic operations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h7)

question: Why is meticulous documentation by the nurse on clinic records particularly important?

options.A: It generates vital epidemiological data for community health planning and tracks individual child progress.
options.B: It serves as a legal contract between the mother and the pharmaceutical manufacturer.
options.C: It replaces the need for verbal communication between healthcare workers.
options.D: It prevents mothers from visiting any other healthcare facility in the country.

explanation: Accurate records allow healthcare teams to track vaccination coverage and child growth trends over time while informing broader public health policies. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h7)

question: What is a major barrier to regular infant welfare clinic attendance in many parts of Nigeria?

options.A: An excessive surplus of pediatric doctors in rural areas
options.B: Complete eradication of all vaccine-preventable diseases
options.C: Mandatory enrollment in international health insurance
options.D: Geographical distance and long waiting times at clinics

explanation: Far distances and lengthy queues discourage caregivers from making regular trips for preventative clinic visits. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h8)

question: Which strategy is most effective for addressing high default rates among registered infants?

options.A: Closing all primary health clinics to force mothers into tertiary hospitals
options.B: Halting all health education talks to speed up daily queue movement
options.C: Punishing parents financially whenever they miss a single vaccination date
options.D: Deploying community health volunteers to track defaulters and conduct outreach services

explanation: Using community-based volunteers to follow up on missed appointments helps bring mothers back into care and bridges gaps in access. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T54#GNS214_U1_T54_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of routine child growth monitoring in primary health care?

options.A: Diagnosing congenital genetic disorders in newborns
options.B: Tracking physical development to detect early growth faltering
options.C: Treating acute infectious diseases during clinic visits
options.D: Providing free nutritional supplements to all children

explanation: Growth monitoring focuses on regular measurements to catch subtle negative changes in a child's weight gain before severe malnutrition develops. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h1)

question: Why is regular growth tracking considered a continuous process rather than a one-time assessment?

options.A: Because Nigerian health policy requires monthly clinic attendance for fines
options.B: Because children change clothes frequently during their first five years
options.C: Because weighing scales lose calibration if they are not used every week
options.D: Because physical growth is dynamic and patterns reveal health trends over time

explanation: A single weight measurement only provides a snapshot, whereas serial measurements show the actual trajectory and velocity of a child's growth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h1)

question: Which anthropometric indicator is primarily used to assess chronic malnutrition and stunting in children?

options.A: Weight-for-Length
options.B: Length-for-Age
options.C: Head Circumference
options.D: Weight-for-Age

explanation: Deficits in length or height relative to age indicate long-term nutritional deprivation and chronic illness, known as stunting. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h2)

question: A child presents with a very low weight relative to their current height. Which condition does this finding most strongly suggest?

options.A: Genetic short stature
options.B: Chronic long-term stunting
options.C: Normal developmental variation
options.D: Acute malnutrition and wasting

explanation: Weight-for-height or weight-for-length specifically measures body mass relative to stature, where low values indicate recent weight loss or wasting. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h2)

question: What must a nurse do with a weighing scale before taking a child's measurement during a clinic session?

options.A: Wipe the scale surface with a dry cloth
options.B: Record the tare weight in the main register
options.C: Place a heavy blanket on the platform
options.D: Adjust and calibrate the scale to zero

explanation: Checking and adjusting the scale to zero before each measurement session eliminates baseline error and ensures accurate readings. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h3)

question: Why must a nurse measure the recumbent length of an infant rather than their standing height?

options.A: Infants under two years cannot stand upright independently for accurate height measurement
options.B: Infants tend to stretch their spine longer when lying down on a flat surface
options.C: Recumbent length provides data for weight-for-age rather than length-for-age indices
options.D: Standing height measurement requires expensive electronic laser equipment not found in clinics

explanation: Children under two years old lack the postural stability required for a valid standing height measurement, making a horizontal measuring board necessary. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h3)

question: What is the correct positioning when reading a mechanical scale dial to avoid measurement error?

options.A: Viewing the indicator from a sharp angle
options.B: Reading the numbers from above while standing
options.C: Guessing the midpoint between two hash marks
options.D: Reading the dial directly at eye level

explanation: Parallax error occurs when a scale pointer is viewed from an angle, making eye-level reading essential for accuracy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h4)

question: How should the assistant position an infant's legs when measuring recumbent length on an infantometer?

options.A: Lift both legs completely off the measuring surface to measure from the hip joints
options.B: Cross the ankles loosely over one another to prevent the infant from kicking the board
options.C: Bend both knees upward toward the chest to keep the infant calm during the procedure
options.D: Gently press the knees down to straighten them while sliding the footplate against the heels

explanation: The knees must be fully extended without causing injury, and the movable footplate brought firmly against the heels to obtain an accurate length. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h4)

question: What does the horizontal axis represent on a standard WHO child growth chart?

options.A: Age of the child
options.B: Weight of the child
options.C: Mid-upper arm circumference
options.D: Length or height

explanation: The horizontal (x-axis) of growth charts displays chronological age, while the vertical (y-axis) displays the physical measurement parameter. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h5)

question: Why is it important to connect the plotted dots from successive clinic visits with a continuous line?

options.A: To visualize the direction and velocity of the child's growth trajectory over time
options.B: To fill in missing data points when a mother misses a scheduled monthly visit
options.C: To determine the exact date when the child will double their birth weight
options.D: To calculate the total weight the child has gained since birth in a single sum

explanation: Connecting the dots forms a growth curve that reveals whether the child is growing along a healthy path or deviating from expected standards. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h5)

question: What term describes a growth curve that flattens or crosses downward across reference lines?

options.A: Normal progression
options.B: Catch-up velocity
options.C: Growth faltering
options.D: Skeletal maturation

explanation: When a child's weight curve flattens or drops across reference lines, it indicates growth faltering requiring prompt nutritional assessment. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h6)

question: A child's weight curve runs completely parallel to the median reference line over four consecutive clinic visits. What does this pattern indicate?

options.A: Severe acute malnutrition requiring immediate therapeutic feeding
options.B: Measurement error caused by an uncalibrated weighing scale
options.C: Chronic stunting caused by prolonged protein-energy deficiency
options.D: Normal, healthy physical growth and steady development

explanation: A curve paralleling the reference standard means the child is gaining weight and growing at the expected rate for their age. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h6)

question: Which common childhood infection cycle frequently contributes to rapid growth faltering in Nigerian children?

options.A: Benign skin pigmentation
options.B: Congenital heart disease
options.C: Diarrhea and malaria
options.D: Seasonal allergic rhinitis

explanation: Frequent infections like diarrhea and malaria increase nutrient loss and metabolic needs while depressing appetite, directly driving weight loss. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a direct cause of nutritional growth faltering in infants?

options.A: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life
options.B: Inappropriate dilution of commercial infant formula
options.C: Delayed introduction of thick complementary foods
options.D: Recurrent episodes of acute watery diarrhea

explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months provides optimal nutrition and protects against infection, supporting healthy growth rather than causing faltering. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h7)

question: What is an essential first step when a nurse counsels a mother whose child exhibits growth faltering?

options.A: Praising positive care practices before exploring feeding routines
options.B: Prescribing high-dose multivitamin syrups without evaluation
options.C: Rebuking the mother for failing to provide adequate meals
options.D: Referring the family immediately to a tertiary nutrition ward

explanation: A supportive, non-judgmental approach builds rapport and encourages the mother to share accurate information about home feeding practices. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h8)

question: Why is scheduling a short-term follow-up visit crucial after identifying growth faltering?

options.A: To punish the caregiver for missing the previous monthly weighing session
options.B: To administer routine childhood vaccines ahead of the national schedule
options.C: To evaluate whether the agreed-upon home feeding and health interventions are working
options.D: To collect user fees for the growth chart booklet issued at birth

explanation: A prompt follow-up allows the nurse to check weight velocity and ensure that the nutritional advice or medical referral has resolved the issue. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T55#GNS214_U1_T55_h8)

question: What stool frequency defines diarrhoea clinically?

options.A: Any single episode of nocturnal defaecation
options.B: Passing hard stools every three days
options.C: One bulky stool containing mucus daily
options.D: Three or more loose or liquid stools per day

explanation: The standard clinical definition relies on a change in stool consistency to loose or liquid combined with a frequency threshold of three or more times daily. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h1)

question: Which clinical feature primarily distinguishes dysentery from acute watery diarrhoea?

options.A: Complete absence of fever or malaise
options.B: Presence of visible blood in the stool
options.C: Total duration exceeding two full weeks
options.D: Response solely to oral rehydration salts

explanation: Acute bloody diarrhoea or dysentery specifically involves mucosal invasion and ulceration, manifesting visibly as red blood in the stool. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h1)

question: What is the primary mechanism of fluid loss in secretory diarrhoea?

options.A: Complete cessation of renal filtration mechanisms
options.B: Osmotic drawing of water by unabsorbed dietary sugars
options.C: Active secretion of electrolytes into the intestinal lumen
options.D: Physical destruction of the entire muscularis layer

explanation: Secretory toxins stimulate active ion transport out of the mucosal cells into the gut lumen, passively pulling large volumes of water with them. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h2)

question: Which acid-base imbalance commonly accompanies severe dehydration from acute watery diarrhoea?

options.A: Respiratory acidosis
options.B: Metabolic alkalosis
options.C: Respiratory alkalosis
options.D: Metabolic acidosis

explanation: Massive gastrointestinal loss of bicarbonate-rich fluids directly precipitates a state of metabolic acidosis in the patient. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h2)

question: Which viral pathogen is the most frequent cause of severe dehydrating diarrhoea in infants?

options.A: Varicella zoster
options.B: Hepatitis A virus
options.C: Cytomegalovirus
options.D: Rotavirus

explanation: Rotavirus historically accounts for the majority of severe, acute dehydrating viral gastroenteritis admissions in young children globally. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h3)

question: Why does early cessation of exclusive breastfeeding increase a child's risk of diarrhoeal disease?

options.A: It removes maternal immunological factors and introduces contaminated substitutes
options.B: It stimulates excessive production of gastric hydrochloric acid
options.C: It causes an immediate permanent closure of the pyloric sphincter
options.D: It prevents the normal physiological absorption of dietary lipids

explanation: Breast milk provides passive immunity and clean nutrition; stopping it early exposes the infant to contaminated water and weaning foods before their immune system is mature. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h3)

question: A child who is lethargic, has very sunken eyes, and a skin pinch that goes back very slowly is classified under which dehydration category?

options.A: No active dehydration
options.B: Chronic malabsorption
options.C: Severe dehydration
options.D: Some dehydration

explanation: Lethargy, very sunken eyes, and a very slow skin recoil are classic IMCI diagnostic markers for severe dehydration requiring immediate rehydration. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h4)

question: What is the clinical significance of a child drinking eagerly and frantically during a fluid assessment?

options.A: It proves the child is suffering from acute upper respiratory infection
options.B: It demonstrates normal physiological satiety after feeding
options.C: It indicates significant fluid deficit classified as some dehydration
options.D: It signals the complete absence of any systemic electrolyte imbalance

explanation: An eager, thirsty response to being offered fluids reflects moderate body water depletion corresponding to the some dehydration category. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h4)

question: What physiological mechanism allows low-osmolarity ORS to work effectively during secretory diarrhoea?

options.A: Sodium-glucose cotransporters remain functional in the intestinal mucosa
options.B: Direct absorption of dry powder through the gastric wall
options.C: High sugar concentrations completely paralyze intestinal peristalsis
options.D: Neutralization of stomach acid by bicarbonate buffers

explanation: The intestinal sodium-glucose linked transporter uses glucose molecules to pull sodium and water across the brush border epithelium regardless of secretory toxin activity. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T56#GNS214_U1_T56_h5)

question: What is the primary therapeutic rationale for prescribing daily zinc supplementation during acute childhood diarrhoea?

question: What is the primary physiological danger associated with acute diarrhoeal disease in young children?

options.D: It prevents the infant from developing childhood respiratory allergies

explanation: Skin-to-skin contact utilizes maternal body heat to prevent neonatal hypothermia, which is a major contributor to newborn morbidity. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T60#GNS214_U1_T60_h5)

question: For how many months is exclusive breastfeeding recommended for a healthy newborn?

options.A: Only during the neonatal period
options.B: First three months of life
options.C: First six months of life
options.D: Until the infant reaches one year

explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding for six months provides complete nourishment and immune protection without needing water or other foods. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T60#GNS214_U1_T60_h6)

question: What is a primary advantage of utilizing community health extension workers in maternal and child health programs?

options.A: Managing hospital blood banks in urban secondary medical centers
options.B: Replacing tertiary obstetric surgeons during complex surgical procedures
options.C: Prescribing advanced oncological drugs for pregnant women at home
options.D: Bridging cultural gaps and providing early recognition and referral from remote areas

explanation: Community workers live among the populace, making them well-positioned to educate families and spot early warning signs requiring urgent transfer. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T60#GNS214_U1_T60_h6)

question: What is the primary public health goal of routine immunization within a Primary Health Care system?

options.A: Diagnosing asymptomatic congenital anomalies early
options.B: Treating chronic illnesses in adult populations
options.C: Preventing communicable diseases through herd immunity
options.D: Providing nutritional supplements to malnourished children

explanation: Routine immunization programs are designed to stimulate immune responses and build herd immunity, effectively stopping the transmission of major communicable diseases at the community level. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h1)

question: Why are Primary Health Care clinics considered the most effective settings for vaccine delivery in Nigeria?

options.A: They mandate compulsory hospitalization for all newborn infants
options.B: They specialize exclusively in the treatment of infectious outbreaks
options.C: They possess advanced laboratory facilities for manufacturing vaccines
options.D: They provide the closest point of community access for routine services

explanation: PHC facilities are strategically positioned at the grassroots level, ensuring that mothers and infants in rural and urban communities can easily access routine vaccinations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h1)

question: What key component is produced during active immunity that ensures long-term protection against a pathogen?

options.A: Exogenous albumin
options.B: Coagulation factors
options.C: Memory cells
options.D: Synthetic platelets

explanation: Active immunity stimulates the body to generate B and T memory cells, which recognize the pathogen rapidly upon future exposure. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h2)

question: An infant receives protective antibodies through breast milk from an immunized mother. What type of immunity does this represent?

options.A: Artificial active immunity
options.B: Natural passive immunity
options.C: Artificial passive immunity
options.D: Natural active immunity

explanation: Transfer of maternal antibodies through breast milk or across the placenta is a natural process that confers immediate, temporary passive immunity to the infant. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h2)

question: Which vaccines are routinely administered to a newborn infant immediately at birth in Nigeria?

options.A: Pentavalent and Pneumococcal
options.B: BCG and Oral Polio Vaccine
options.C: Rotavirus and Inactivated Polio
options.D: Measles and Yellow Fever

explanation: At birth, infants receive the BCG vaccine for tuberculosis protection and the zero dose of the Oral Polio Vaccine. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h3)

question: A mother brings her healthy 14-week-old infant to the PHC clinic for routine immunization. Which set of vaccines is due for this visit?

options.A: Second doses of Pentavalent and booster doses of Tetanus toxoid
options.B: Zero doses of OPV and routine administration of Vitamin A
options.C: Third doses of Pentavalent, OPV, PCV, Rotavirus, plus IPV
options.D: First doses of Measles, Yellow Fever, and BCG

explanation: According to the national immunization schedule, the 14-week visit requires the third series of Pentavalent, OPV, PCV, Rotavirus, along with the first dose of Inactivated Polio Vaccine. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h3)

question: What is the primary pathological consequence of wild poliovirus infection in children?

options.A: Progressive renal tubular necrosis
options.B: Severe generalized skin necrosis
options.C: Irreversible acute flaccid paralysis
options.D: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

explanation: Poliovirus targets the motor neurons in the spinal cord, resulting in sudden, irreversible muscle weakness and paralysis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h4)

question: Which clinical feature is most characteristic of clinical measles infection in young children?

options.A: Asymmetrical muscle weakness starting in the lower limbs
options.B: Generalized maculopapular rash preceded by fever and cough
options.C: Persistent watery diarrhea with severe electrolyte wasting
options.D: Painful swelling of the parotid salivary glands

explanation: Measles typically presents with prodromal fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, followed by a characteristic maculopapular rash spreading downward from the head. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h4)

question: What is the acceptable temperature range for storing refrigerator-sensitive routine vaccines like Pentavalent and PCV?

options.B: +2°C to +8°C

explanation: Refrigerated vaccines must be kept strictly between +2°C and +8°C to prevent thermal damage or accidental freezing. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h5)

question: What happens to toxoid and adjuvanted vaccines such as Pentavalent if they are accidentally exposed to freezing temperatures in the cold room?

options.A: They become hyper-potent and induce stronger immunity
options.B: They remain safe to use once they return to room temperature
options.C: They suffer irreversible potency loss and must be discarded
options.D: Their expiration date is automatically extended by six months

explanation: Adjuvanted vaccines containing aluminum components permanently clump and lose potency when frozen, rendering them ineffective. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h5)

question: Which anatomical site is recommended for intramuscular vaccine administration in infants under one year of age?

options.A: Anterolateral aspect of the thigh
options.B: Ventral gluteal site of the hip
options.C: Deltoid muscle of the upper arm
options.D: Dorsogluteal muscle of the buttocks

explanation: The vastus lateralis muscle in the anterolateral thigh is the preferred site for infant IM injections to avoid sciatic nerve injury and ensure adequate muscle mass. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h6)

question: What is the expected immediate visual sign of a correctly performed intradermal BCG injection?

options.A: Rapid pooling of blood at the injection orifice
options.B: A raised, blanched wheal with a pitted surface
options.C: Complete disappearance of fluid without skin reaction
options.D: Immediate deep subcutaneous hematoma formation

explanation: A correct intradermal injection raises a small, pale, orange-peel-like wheal at the insertion site. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h6)

question: What classification applies to an adverse event caused by an incorrect dilution technique or unsterile injection practice?

options.A: Intrinsic vaccine reaction
options.B: Coincidental medical illness
options.C: Idiopathic hypersensitivity
options.D: Program error-induced event

explanation: Events resulting from mistakes in vaccine preparation, handling, or administration are classified as immunization program errors. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h7)

question: A mother returns to the clinic alarmed because her infant developed a mild fever and localized tenderness hours after receiving the Pentavalent vaccine. How should the nurse respond?

options.A: Reassure the mother that these are common, expected mild reactions
options.B: Report the case immediately as a severe vaccine manufacturing failure
options.C: Withhold all subsequent scheduled vaccine doses permanently
options.D: Admit the child to the inpatient ward for intravenous antibiotics

explanation: Mild systemic and local responses like low-grade fever and soreness are normal immune responses that resolve spontaneously within a few days. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h7)

question: What term describes the delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite the availability of vaccination services?

options.A: Seroconversion delay
options.B: Cold chain failure
options.C: Immunological tolerance
options.D: Vaccine hesitancy

explanation: Vaccine hesitancy refers to behavioral reluctance or refusal to vaccinate despite service accessibility. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h8)

question: Which strategy is most effective for a nurse seeking to improve routine immunization uptake in a rural community with high suspicion of new vaccines?

options.A: Relying solely on printed flyers distributed in urban centers
options.B: Enforcing mandatory legal penalties on uncooperative parents
options.C: Withholding general healthcare services until compliance improves
options.D: Engaging community and religious leaders for localized health talks

explanation: Involving respected community gatekeepers builds local trust and addresses cultural concerns much more effectively than punitive measures. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T61#GNS214_U1_T61_h8)

question: What is the primary immunological mechanism by which vaccines prevent infectious diseases?

options.A: Providing passive antibodies through intravenous infusion
options.B: Stimulating the host immune system to produce memory cells
options.C: Directly destroying pathogens within the gastrointestinal tract
options.D: Altering the genetic code of resident normal flora

explanation: Vaccines work by safely introducing antigens that stimulate the host's immune system to produce active immunity through memory B and T cells without causing the disease itself. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h1)

question: Which of the following best describes the concept of herd immunity in vaccine-preventable diseases?

options.A: Immunity acquired exclusively through breast milk in infants
options.B: Protection of vulnerable unvaccinated individuals when a high percentage of the population is immunized
options.C: Resistance developed after recovering from a natural clinical infection
options.D: The mandatory isolation of herds or groups during an epidemic outbreak

explanation: Herd immunity occurs when high vaccination coverage in a population indirectly protects vulnerable, unvaccinated individuals by drastically reducing the spread of the pathogen. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h1)

question: Which vaccines are routinely administered to a newborn infant at birth in Nigeria according to the national schedule?

options.A: Measles and Yellow Fever vaccines
options.B: Pentavalent and Rotavirus vaccines
options.C: BCG and Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV zero dose)
options.D: Tetanus toxoid and Meningococcal vaccines

explanation: At birth, the Nigerian routine immunization schedule mandates the administration of BCG for tuberculosis and the birth dose (zero dose) of the oral polio vaccine. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h2)

question: At what age are infants in Nigeria typically scheduled to receive the measles vaccine for the first time?

options.A: At birth
options.B: At 6 weeks
options.C: At 9 months
options.D: At 18 months

explanation: The routine immunization schedule in Nigeria specifies that the first dose of the measles vaccine should be given when the infant reaches 9 months of age. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h2)

question: What is the primary clinical benefit of administering the BCG vaccine to a newborn infant?

options.A: Complete eradication of pulmonary tuberculosis infection later in life
options.B: Prevention of severe, disseminated forms of tuberculosis such as meningitis
options.C: Immunity against viral respiratory tract infections
options.D: Immediate cure for congenital maternal tuberculosis

explanation: While BCG does not prevent primary pulmonary infection, it provides vital protection against severe, life-threatening disseminated forms of tuberculosis in children, such as tuberculous meningitis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h3)

question: What type of clinical syndrome must nurses actively surveil and report as part of polio eradication efforts?

options.A: Acute flaccid paralysis (AFP)
options.B: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
options.C: Severe acute malnutrition
options.D: Hypertensive crisis

explanation: Acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) surveillance is the gold standard used by healthcare workers to detect potential cases of poliomyelitis in the community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h3)

question: Which characteristic clinical sign is produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae in the pharynx of an infected child?

options.A: Watery vesicles on the buccal mucosa
options.B: A greyish pseudomembrane that can obstruct the airway
options.C: Bleeding gingival ulcers with purulent discharge
options.D: White painless patches resembling oral thrush

explanation: Diphtheria is characterized by the formation of a tough, greyish pseudomembrane in the pharynx, which can lead to airway obstruction and suffocation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h4)

question: How is neonatal tetanus typically transmitted to an infant in communities with poor hygiene practices?

options.A: Inhalation of respiratory droplets from an infected sibling
options.B: Ingestion of unpasteurized cow milk during the first week of life
options.C: Contamination of the unhealed umbilical cord stump during or after delivery
options.D: Insect vector bites during the rainy season

explanation: Neonatal tetanus occurs when Clostridium tetani spores contaminate the umbilical cord stump, often due to unhygienic instruments or traditional substances applied during or after delivery. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h4)

question: What are the characteristic pathognomonic oral findings often seen in the prodromal phase of measles?

options.A: Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa
options.B: Strawberry tongue with enlarged papillae
options.C: White pseudomembranes on the tonsils
options.D: Ulcerative vesicles on the hard palate

explanation: Koplik spots—small white spots on a red background located on the buccal mucosa—are classic pathognomonic signs appearing before the generalized measles rash. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h5)

question: How is the yellow fever virus primarily transmitted to humans?

options.A: Ingestion of contaminated municipal water
options.B: Inhalation of aerosolized droplets from livestock
options.C: Bites from infected Aedes mosquitoes
options.D: Direct contact with skin lesions of an infected person

explanation: Yellow fever is an arboviral disease transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h5)

question: Which physical sign is indicative of meningeal irritation when assessing a patient for suspected meningitis?

options.A: Positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs
options.B: Inability to perform rapid alternating hand movements
options.C: Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities
options.D: Asymmetrical facial drooping when smiling

explanation: Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are classic clinical indicators of meningeal irritation evaluated during physical examinations of patients with suspected meningitis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h6)

question: Why is Nigeria particularly vulnerable to outbreaks of meningococcal meningitis during certain periods of the year?

options.B: It is located within the geographical region known as the African meningitis belt
options.C: High humidity and heavy rainfall during the monsoon season favor bacterial growth
options.D: Universal cessation of meningococcal vaccination occurs nationwide annually
options.A: Widespread consumption of raw dairy products during harvest seasons

explanation: Nigeria lies within the African 'meningitis belt,' making the population highly susceptible to seasonal bacterial meningitis epidemics, especially during the dry harmattan months. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h6)

question: What is the most reliable method for a nurse to verify a child's previous immunization status during a clinical assessment?

options.A: Relying solely on the mother's oral recall of vaccination dates
options.B: Checking the home-based health record or immunization card
options.C: Inspecting the child's skin for injection scar marks
options.D: Ordering a complete blood count and serum antibody titer

explanation: The home-based health record, or immunization card, is the most reliable document for verifying a child's exact vaccination history and scheduling future doses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h7)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take when a child presents with clinical symptoms strongly suggestive of a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease like measles?

options.A: Send the child home immediately without examination
options.B: Institute appropriate isolation and infection control precautions
options.C: Administer an immediate therapeutic dose of oral polio vaccine
options.D: Wait for laboratory confirmation before notifying public health officials

explanation: Isolating the patient and utilizing proper infection control precautions prevents nosocomial transmission of highly contagious diseases within the healthcare facility. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h7)

question: What is the recommended temperature range for storing most routine refrigerated vaccines within the cold chain system?

options.B: +2°C to +8°C

explanation: Most routine refrigerated vaccines must be maintained strictly within a cold chain temperature range of +2°C to +8°C to preserve their potency and efficacy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h8)

question: Who is the primary local government officer to whom Nigerian nurses report suspected cases of vaccine-preventable diseases for surveillance?

options.A: The Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO)
options.B: The Director of Budget and Planning
options.C: The Local Government Education Secretary
options.D: The Chief Pharmacist of the State Depot

explanation: The Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO) at the LGA level is responsible for receiving reports of notifiable diseases from healthcare facilities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h8)

question: What is an effective nursing approach when addressing vaccine hesitancy caused by cultural or religious misconceptions in a community?

options.A: Scolding parents for neglecting their parental responsibilities
options.B: Engaging community leaders and conducting respectful, transparent dialogue
options.C: Withholding general healthcare services until the child is vaccinated
options.D: Ignoring parental concerns and administering vaccines without consent

explanation: Engaging community leaders and fostering respectful, transparent communication helps build trust and effectively addresses the root causes of vaccine hesitancy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h9)

question: How should a nurse counsel a mother who expresses worry over her infant developing mild fever and site soreness after receiving the pentavalent vaccine?

options.A: Advise immediate hospitalization in the intensive care unit
options.B: Explain that these are normal, expected mild side effects indicating the immune system is responding
options.C: Instruct the mother never to bring the child for subsequent immunization doses
options.D: Prescribe a heavy course of broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Normal mild reactions like low-grade fever and soreness should be explained to caregivers as expected signs that the immune system is actively building protection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T62#GNS214_U1_T62_h9)

question: What is the primary goal of Universal Child Immunization (UCI)?

options.A: To treat chronic illnesses in children
options.B: To ensure every infant receives a full course of routine immunizations before one year of age
options.C: to eradicate adult infectious diseases globally
options.D: To provide nutritional support for malnourished infants

explanation: UCI specifically focuses on ensuring that every infant receives a full course of routine immunizations against major childhood infectious diseases before reaching the age of one year. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h1)

question: How does immunization protect vulnerable infants who cannot yet be vaccinated?

options.A: Through passive transfer of synthetic drugs
options.B: By establishing herd immunity when coverage is high enough
options.C: By isolating the infant from all community members
options.D: Through mandatory antibiotic administration

explanation: When vaccination coverage reaches a high threshold in a population, herd immunity is established, providing indirect protection to vulnerable infants who are too young for vaccines. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h1)

question: Why is immunization considered a cornerstone of Primary Health Care (PHC)?

options.A: It is an expensive hospital-based procedure
options.B: It is one of the most cost-effective interventions to prevent disease and reduce hospital admissions
options.C: It completely replaces the need for nutritional counseling
options.D: It focuses exclusively on treating acute infections

explanation: Immunization is a cost-effective public health tool that prevents diseases and lowers overall healthcare costs and hospital admissions within the PHC framework. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h2)

question: What does integrating immunization into PHC clinic visits allow nurses to do?

options.A: Prescribe complex surgical procedures
options.B: Identify missed opportunities for vaccination and monitor growth charts
options.C: Discontinue all maternal care programs
options.D: Isolate healthy children from the community

explanation: Routine encounters allow nurses to assess overall health, check growth charts, and catch up on any missed vaccine doses during primary care visits. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h2)

question: Which vaccine is typically administered at birth according to the Nigerian National Immunization Schedule?

options.A: Measles-rubella vaccine
options.B: BCG and Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV zero)
options.C: Pentavalent vaccine
options.D: Rotavirus vaccine

explanation: According to the national schedule, BCG and the birth dose of oral polio vaccine (OPV zero) are given immediately at birth. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h3)

question: Why is it important for nurses to follow the chronological age guidelines in the immunization schedule?

options.A: To ensure children are protected during their most vulnerable developmental stages
options.B: To reduce the cost of vaccine manufacturing
options.C: To shorten the duration of clinic opening hours
options.D: To eliminate the need for cold chain storage

explanation: Following the precise schedule ensures infants develop timely immunity when they are most susceptible to vaccine-preventable diseases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of cold chain management in immunization?

options.A: To freeze all vaccines solid before transport
options.B: To store and transport vaccines within safe temperature ranges to preserve potency
options.C: To test vaccines for bacterial contamination in the field
options.D: To accelerate the manufacturing process of new vaccines

explanation: Cold chain management ensures vaccines are kept at correct temperatures so they do not lose their potency before being administered. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h4)

question: Which inventory management rule should nurses practice to prevent vaccine wastage?

options.A: First-expiry, first-out (FEFO)
options.B: Last-in, first-out (LIFO)
options.C: Random selection method
options.D: Storage based on alphabetical order

explanation: The first-expiry, first-out (FEFO) rule ensures that vaccines expiring sooner are used before those with later expiration dates. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h4)

question: What is defined as a vaccine contraindication?

options.A: A mild cold with a low-grade fever
options.B: A condition that significantly increases the risk of a serious adverse reaction
options.C: Current administration of oral antibiotics
options.D: The child being in the recovery phase of a minor illness

explanation: A contraindication is a medical condition or history that elevates the risk of a severe adverse reaction, such as anaphylaxis, if the vaccine is given. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h5)

question: How should a nurse handle a child presenting with a mild acute illness and no high fever during an immunization visit?

options.A: Refuse vaccination entirely and reschedule for three months later
options.B: Proceed with vaccination, as mild illness is generally not a contraindication
options.C: Administer broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics first
options.D: Refer the child immediately to a tertiary surgical unit

explanation: Mild acute illnesses do not contraindicate routine vaccination; deferring vaccination in such cases leads to missed opportunities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h5)

question: What is the preferred anatomical site for intramuscular vaccine injections in infants?

options.A: Gluteus maximus muscle
options.B: Vastus lateralis muscle of the anterolateral thigh
options.C: Deltoid muscle of the arm
options.D: Abdominal wall subcutaneous tissue

explanation: The vastus lateralis muscle in the thigh is the preferred site for infants because it provides adequate muscle mass and avoids major nerves and vessels. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h6)

question: What immediate action must a nurse take with a used injection needle after giving a vaccine?

options.A: Recap the needle carefully using both hands
options.B: Place the needle and syringe directly into a puncture-resistant safety box
options.C: Leave the syringe on the tray for disposal at the end of the shift
options.D: Break the needle off by hand before discarding

explanation: Used sharps must be immediately dropped into a puncture-resistant safety box without recapping to prevent needle-stick injuries. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h6)

question: Which of the following is classified as an immunization error-related AEFI?

options.A: A mild fever occurring naturally after a live attenuated vaccine
options.B: An adverse event caused by incorrect reconstitution or improper administration technique
options.C: An underlying congenital heart defect discovered coincidentally after vaccination
options.D: A mild rash resulting from an expected genetic allergy to vaccine stabilizers

explanation: An immunization error-related AEFI stems from mistakes in handling, preparing, or administering the vaccine, such as wrong dosage or incorrect route. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h7)

question: What is the immediate pharmacological intervention for a child experiencing acute anaphylaxis after vaccination?

options.A: Oral paracetamol syrup
options.B: Intramuscular epinephrine
options.C: Intravenous routine saline infusion without drugs
options.D: Topical hydrocortisone cream

explanation: Intramuscular epinephrine is the drug of choice for the immediate emergency treatment of severe anaphylactic reactions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h7)

question: How is vaccine hesitancy best defined?

options.A: Total absence of any vaccination clinics in a country
options.B: Delay in acceptance or refusal of vaccines despite availability of services
options.C: The physical inability to maintain cold chain temperatures
options.D: A severe allergic reaction occurring immediately after an injection

explanation: Vaccine hesitancy describes a reluctance or refusal to vaccinate despite accessible services, often influenced by misinformation and lack of confidence. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h8)

question: What is an effective strategy for a nurse addressing vaccine hesitancy in a local Nigerian community?

options.A: Scolding caregivers who ask skeptical questions about vaccines
options.B: Partnering with local leaders and using respectful, culturally tailored dialogue
options.C: Withholding all healthcare services until compliance is 100 percent
options.D: Relying strictly on written pamphlets without verbal communication

explanation: Engaging community leaders and using empathetic, culturally sensitive communication builds trust and effectively counters misinformation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h8)

question: Which document serves as the primary home-based record for a child's vaccination history?

options.A: The clinic tally sheet
options.B: The child health card
options.C: The cold chain temperature log
options.D: The national census report

explanation: The child health card is kept at home by the caregiver and serves as the primary longitudinal record of the child's immunization milestones. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h9)

question: Why is recording the vaccine batch number important during an immunization session?

options.A: To calculate the financial cost of the clinic session
options.B: To ensure traceability and assist in AEFI investigations if safety issues arise
options.C: To determine the child's exact chronological age
options.D: To replace the need for cold chain temperature monitoring

explanation: Recording batch numbers ensures full traceability of vaccine lots, which is crucial for tracking and investigating adverse events following immunization. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T63#GNS214_U1_T63_h9)

question: Which agency currently oversees the integration and administration of the National Programme on Immunization in Nigeria?

options.A: National Primary Health Care Development Agency
options.B: Nigerian Medical Association
options.C: National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control
options.D: Federal Ministry of Women Affairs

explanation: The NPI was integrated into the NPHCDA to ensure routine vaccines are delivered alongside other primary healthcare services at the community level. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T64#GNS214_U1_T64_h1)

question: What was the primary organizational goal behind absorbing the independent immunization agency into the primary health care framework?

options.A: To transfer complete operational control to private pharmaceutical firms
options.B: To increase the market cost of importing international biological products
options.C: To streamline vaccine delivery alongside comprehensive community health services
options.D: To restrict vaccination access exclusively to federal tertiary medical centers

explanation: Merging the program into primary healthcare structures allows routine immunization to reach remote populations by utilizing existing local health clinics. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T64#GNS214_U1_T64_h1)

question: By what age should an eligible infant ideally complete the standard Nigerian routine immunization schedule?

options.A: At exactly two years of age
options.B: Prior to starting secondary education
options.C: By the end of the third month
options.D: Before their first birthday

explanation: Standard immunization schedules aim to fully protect infants during their most vulnerable first year of life against deadly infectious diseases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T64#GNS214_U1_T64_h2)

question: Why is the involvement of traditional and religious leaders emphasized in achieving immunization objectives across rural Nigerian communities?

options.A: They are legally mandated to procure cold chain equipment for local health posts
options.B: They hold significant influence over community acceptance and health-seeking behaviors
options.C: They possess formal clinical training required to administer injectable vaccines
options.D: They manage the financial allocation of international donor funds directly

explanation: Community gatekeepers and leaders build local trust, helping to overcome vaccine hesitancy and cultural skepticism. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T64#GNS214_U1_T64_h2)

question: At which visit interval is the Pentavalent vaccine routinely completed for an infant in Nigeria?

options.A: 24 hours
options.B: 14 weeks
options.C: Birth
options.D: 9 months

explanation: The three-dose primary series of the Pentavalent vaccine is administered at ages 6, 10, and 14 weeks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T64#GNS214_U1_T64_h3)

question: A nursing student preparing for clinicals notes that the BCG vaccine is given at birth. What is the primary target disease for this biological product?

options.A: Poliomyelitis
options.B: Measles
options.C: Tetanus
options.D: Tuberculosis

explanation: BCG (Bacille Calmette-Guérin) is a live-attenuated vaccine specifically designed to protect infants against severe forms of tuberculosis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T64#GNS214_U1_T64_h3)

question: What is the standard safe temperature range for storing routine vaccines in facility-level refrigerators?

options.B: 0°C to -4°C
options.C: +2°C to +8°C

explanation: Most routine vaccines must be maintained between +2°C and +8°C to prevent heat degradation without freezing them. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T64#GNS214_U1_T64_h4)

question: Why is the shake test performed on frozen-suspected vials of pentavalent or tetanus toxoid vaccines?

options.A: To determine if the vaccine has been previously exposed to freezing temperatures which ruins potency
options.B: To test the structural integrity of the glass ampoule prior to needle aspiration
options.C: To check if the Vaccine Vial Monitor has changed its color to dark blue
options.D: To mix the live viral components evenly before oral administration to neonates
